Macrons

Consonantal i

Body, health & movement

hiccup noun and verb

also hiccups, hiccough, have hiccups

classical

Sen. Ep. 47.3: tussis, sternūmenta, singultus

singultus, singultūs m.

noun, fourth declension

a hiccup; hiccups; also a sob

Seneca lists the noises that slaves serving at dinner were beaten for, even involuntary ones: coughing, sneezing, hiccups.

Examples

  • Singultīs? Bibe paulum aquae.

    Hiccups? Drink a little water.composed

  • Anētum quoque ructūs movet … singultūs cohibet.

    Dill also brings up wind … and stops hiccups: a herbal remedy.Plin. NH 20.196

  • singultūs sēdat

    it settles hiccups (of another plant)Plin. NH 21.120

Other words

  • singultiō, singultīre — have hiccups

    verb, fourth conjugation, intransitive · classical · Cels. 5.26; Plin. NH 23.48: singultientibus

  • singultō, singultāre — hiccup; mostly of sobbing

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Quint. 10.7.10: singultantium modō

See also burp, tickle, herbal tea.

SourcesLewis & Short: singultus · Lewis & Short: singultio · Lewis & Short: singulto · Lewis & Short: anethum

Quotations checked against the Perseus Latin texts: Seneca’s letters, Celsus, and Pliny’s Natural History in Mayhoff’s section numbers. Traupman and Morgan–Owens do not have these words in the sections swept; they come from Lewis & Short.
